### 2.1.4 Inner products

An inner product is a function which takes as input two vectors $|v\rangle$ and $|w\rangle$ from a vector space and produces a complex number as output.
For the time being, it will be convenient to write the inner product of $|v\rangle$ and $|w\rangle$ as $(|v\rangle,|w\rangle)$.
This is not the standard quantum mechanical notation; for pedagogical clarity the ($\cdot, \cdot$) notation will be useful occasionally in this chapter.
The standard quantum mechanical notation for the inner product $(|v\rangle,|w\rangle)$ is $\langle v \mid w\rangle$, where $|v\rangle$ and $|w\rangle$ are vectors in the inner product space, and the notation $\langle v|$ is used for the dual vector to the vector $|v\rangle$; the dual is a linear operator from the inner product space $V$ to the complex numbers $\mathbf{C}$, defined by $\langle v|(|w\rangle) \equiv\langle v \mid w\rangle \equiv(|v\rangle,|w\rangle)$.
We will see shortly that the matrix representation of dual vectors is just a row vector.

A function $(\cdot, \cdot)$ from $V \times V$ to $\mathbf{C}$ is an inner product if it satisfies the requirements that:
(1) $(\cdot, \cdot)$ is linear in the second argument,

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(|v\rangle, \sum_{i} \lambda_{i}\left|w_{i}\right\rangle\right)=\sum_{i} \lambda_{i}\left(|v\rangle,\left|w_{i}\right\rangle\right) . \tag{2.13}
\end{equation*}
$$

(2) $(|v\rangle,|w\rangle)=(|w\rangle,|v\rangle)^{*}$.
(3) $(|v\rangle,|v\rangle) \geq 0$ with equality if and only if $|v\rangle=0$.

For example, $\mathbf{C}^{n}$ has an inner product defined by

$$
\left(\left(y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n}\right),\left(z_{1}, \ldots, z_{n}\right)\right) \equiv \sum_{i} y_{i}^{*} z_{i}=\left[y_{1}^{*} \ldots y_{n}^{*}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}
z_{1}  \tag{2.14}\\
\vdots \\
z_{n}
\end{array}\right]
$$

We call a vector space equipped with an inner product an inner product space.
